stem:
A GP reviews an 80-year-old man with established dementia with Lewy bodies who already takes rivastigmine. Most evenings he sees a small dog in the room. He knows that others cannot see it, finds it pleasant and is not frightened. His attention and function are at his usual level, and a review finds no new medical problem or medicine. His daughter is upset and asks for haloperidol to stop the visions.

What is the best response?

options.label: A
options.text: Leave the visions untreated and monitor for distress
options.explanation: The hallucinations cause him no distress or risk, so no drug is needed. Explain this to his daughter and review if distress, agitation or safety problems develop.

options.label: B
options.text: Start low-dose haloperidol and review in one week
options.explanation: People with Lewy body dementia can have severe, sometimes fatal, sensitivity reactions to antipsychotics; haloperidol is particularly hazardous.

options.label: C
options.text: Start risperidone, as the visions are persistent
options.explanation: Persistence alone is not a reason to treat, and risperidone carries the same antipsychotic sensitivity risk.

options.label: D
options.text: Add benzatropine to haloperidol to prevent rigidity
options.explanation: Adding an anticholinergic does not remove the sensitivity risk and may worsen confusion.

options.label: E
options.text: Give bedtime diazepam to lessen the visions
options.explanation: A benzodiazepine will not remove the visions and increases sedation, falls and confusion.

context: In dementia with Lewy bodies, treat hallucinations only when they cause distress or risk, and avoid haloperidol because of severe antipsychotic sensitivity.
